name: Reversing regenerative furnace
summary: The regenerative furnace stores exhaust heat in brick chambers and uses it to warm incoming air, switching the flow direction periodically.
description: A furnace alternates the flow through heat-storing refractory chambers: exhaust heats one chamber while incoming combustion fluid is warmed by another, and the directions are periodically reversed.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

impact.note: Fuel saving and higher heat for furnaces across many societies, from which open-hearth steelmaking and glass tank furnaces grew.

why: Furnaces wasted much of their heat in hot exhaust gases, so recovering it promised large fuel savings for steel and glass works.

market.note: The process can be supplied or used in economic production, separately from the date of its first offer.

date.label: By 13 July 1857
date.basis: The 1857 report describes a six-day comparison at the named works beginning 13 July; the date is an upper bound on actual use, not a first-start date.

events.statement: A regenerative furnace was in use to heat iron and steel at Marriott and Atkinson’s Sheffield works by the start of a reported comparison on 13 July 1857.
events.scope: A reversing regenerative heating furnace operating at Marriott and Atkinson’s steelworks; combustion air is preheated in refractory regenerators.
applications: heating iron and steel for rolling
events.caveats: The contemporary report says the Sheffield furnace operated, and dates a six-day trial beginning 13 July 1857; its exact start and later duration are unknown. It describes alternating heated chambers and incoming air, without establishing the later gas-fired glass-furnace layout. The separately documented Chance adoption was in 1861; neither is asserted to be the world’s first use or first sale.
